stories.headline: Scoreless Leafs rookie McKenna on slow start: 'Still believe in myself'
stories.summary: Maple Leafs rookie Gavin McKenna is experiencing first-hand the pressure of being a first overall pick -- one who still hasn't scored an NHL point.
stories.body:
Gavin McKenna is experiencing firsthand the pressure of being a first overall pick -- one who still hasn't scored an NHL point.

The Maple Leafs forward -- selected first off the board in last June's NHL entry draft -- is looking to hit the scoresheet as Toronto heads into its fourth game of the season Tuesday against Nashville. Failing to register offensively so far -- with three shots on net and a minus-3 rating -- hasn't gone unnoticed by anyone, and McKenna is hearing critical feedback already just a week into his rookie year.

It hasn't exactly been that "welcome to the NHL moment" he'd been hoping for.

"Especially in the Toronto media, putting up zero points in three games, I think you hear about it," McKenna said following the Leafs' optional morning skate Tuesday. "So maybe that's my welcome to the league [thing]. And then I think just [realizing how] hard it is. You come in; you believe in yourself [to produce]. And I still believe in myself ... but it's obviously not where you want to be."

McKenna will have another chance to prove he's no offensive slouch when Toronto takes on the Predators, with McKenna projected to stay on the Leafs' second line with John Tavares and William Nylander. Tavares -- a first overall pick himself by the New York Islanders in 2009 -- has taken McKenna under his wing on and off the ice, inviting the 18-year-old to live with him and his family. McKenna said Tavares has been a valuable sounding board in navigating this opening stretch of his NHL career.

"After every game, we go home and we chat and run through the game," McKenna said. "He's been awesome. He's helped me. With playing on a line [too], we get to talk a lot. When he points things out that we can both work on, I think it helps me a lot. And when he says something, you focus on it, and you realize how smart a player he is. And he's obviously been through it, so he's someone you want to listen to. I trust him a lot."

This isn't the first slow start McKenna has gone through in recent years. He transitioned from the Western Hockey League to the NCAA level last year, for his one and only season at Penn State, and it took time there too for McKenna to get rolling. Once he did, the winger was unstoppable and finished the year with 15 goals and 51 points in 35 games as the Big 10 Freshman of the Year.

McKenna sounds confident he can overcome the new challenges of pro hockey with, eventually, similarly strong results.

"At the end of the day, I've been on many streaks where I've put up no points," he said. "I had a tough start to college last year and then started to figure things out there. I think just honestly learning from last year and learning from these first few games, I think that is going to be key. Sticking with it, being confident. I know it's going to come, so just keep working and have confidence."

It's McKenna's creativity with the puck -- and how he's used that to become a consistent offensive threat in the past -- that set him apart when Toronto was deciding on a top pick last spring. Like many first-year players before him, McKenna is adapting to what bigger, faster competition means and how few windows of opportunity there are to actually make a positive impact during his shifts.

"It's a tough league, and there's not a whole lot of time and space [and] those chances to find the middle of the ice don't come very often," McKenna said. "You've got to make sure you're there and you're ready when you get that chance. And just being simple. I think in juniors and in college, you can get away with trying to make moves at the blue line and not getting the puck deep. But here, you only get so many chances [in] a game and if you don't make that play, then the puck's probably back in your own end, and you're playing in the D zone, and then you're off the ice. So, you got to be smart with your decisions."

McKenna is a true student of the game and has been putting in extra time with Leafs assistant coach Daniel Alfredsson in the video room to zero in on where he can make improvements. When there are extra developmental sessions for McKenna to take advantage of -- like participating in Tuesday's optional on-ice work -- he's in on that as well.

What Toronto's coach Jim Hiller advises for McKenna is to keep his work ethic high -- and screen time low. Anything to avoid letting the outside noise get in any further.

"What you need to do is really stay focused in the moment and stay in the present," Hiller said. "I'm sure that's an evolution for all players. Probably some are better at that than others. But over time, you probably improve in that area, just like any other area of being a professional. We know what we see [from him], and we've looked at it over and over and over again and thought about it. Sometimes it's important to get the player's perspective and see what they see. Hopefully, it lines up with what you see. If it doesn't, then it starts a really good conversation. Usually, it's a two-way street. I know [Alfredsson] has been doing some work with him that way."

stories.headline: NBA preseason buzz: Latest on trades, news and intel
stories.summary: The NBA regular season is just a few weeks away, and we're tracking all the news, deals, and trades across the league.
stories.body:
With preseason games already underway, the 2026-27 NBA season is only a few weeks away from tipping off.

How will LeBron James and Jaylen Brown look on the court in their new Philadelphia 76ers uniforms? What will Giannis Antetokounmpo's first season away from Milwaukee look like? And how will the other new faces in new places make their impact this season?

Check back here for all the latest buzz, news and reactions from our ESPN NBA insiders, with the latest info at the top:

Quick links:

Free agency grades | Trade grades

Trade tracker | Transactions | Offseason buzz

Depth charts | Trade machine | More

Oct. 6

Porzingis injury timetable still 'indefinite'
ESPN's Anthony Slater reported on NBA Today that Golden State Warriors' center Kristaps Porzingis' timetable to return from an undisclosed health issue is still indefinite.

The ramifications of the Hukporti injury for Philadelphia
The season ending Achilles injury to Ariel Hukporti has roster ramifications for the 76ers.

Philadelphia is $1.8 million below the first apron, so they are not allowed to sign a player with their open roster spot until Dec. 4. The 76ers could create financial flexibility but at the cost of Jabari Walker, whose $2.6 million salary is guaranteed for only $250,000. Walker scored 11 points and grabbed 11 rebounds in their pre-season opener.

The 76ers do have an open two-way spot and can sign a player with three years or less in service.

Beyond starter Joel Embiid, Philadelphia's frontcourt depth is Dean Wade, Adem Bona, Dominick Barlow and Walker. -- Bobby Marks

Charania: Hukporti sustained a season-ending ruptured Achilles

An MRI confirm Tuesday that Philadelphia 76ers' center Ariel Hukporti sustained a season-ending torn right Achilles, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Hukporti will undergo surgery for the injury later today.

Doncic, who 'worked his butt off all summer,' lights up Kings
A lighter Luka Doncic scored an easy 21 first-half points in the Los Angeles Lakers' preseason opener over the Sacramento Kings on Monday night, needing only 16 minutes to sharpen up his game in a 127-103 blowout in Sacramento.
Doncic was listed at 244 pounds prior to the 2025-26 season. That dipped to 230 pounds entering training camp. The difference in physique from his heavier days is obvious.

"The guy worked his butt off all summer staying in shape and actually ran this summer," coach JJ Redick said. "He actually did like sprints and stuff. Came into camp in fantastic shape."

The Lakers were without Austin Reaves and Walker Kessler in the preseason opener. Reaves tweaked his ankle recently, and Kessler jammed a finger on the backboard. Both are listed as day-to-day. Without either, the Lakers still rolled through the Kings. Doncic scored all 21 of his points in a 73-point Lakers first half, resting while the backups finished the job. He made three 3s, four shots in the paint and got to the line for nine free throws.

"For someone who normally plays a ton of live basketball [in the summer], he didn't do as much of that by design," Redick said. "We've seen him literally every day in camp incrementally get more and more in rhythm."

Doncic badly strained his hamstring in early April and missed the entire Lakers playoff run while rehabbing the injury. He said he felt "great" against the Kings but downplayed any larger changes to his training regimen.

"I feel probably a little more rested," Doncic said. "I didn't play [on the Slovenian] national team." -- Anthony Slater

Windhorst on Dylan Harper's role with the Spurs: "The Spurs internally believe Dylan Harper is their second-best player. I'm not saying Mitch Johnson's going to come out and say that. He shouldn't come out and say that. That's not a slight on De'Aaron Fox. That's not a slight on Stephon Castle. Harper is a stud.

"You talk to other front offices in the league, they say the same thing. This guy is I mean, look, he's the No. 2 pick in the draft. Of course he's a stud, and he only got better as the season went along."

MacMahon on on Kyrie Irving's expectations in Dallas: "Masai [Ujiri] did not want to have any discussions about Kyrie trades this year. What I can tell you right now is Kyrie is fully on board and excited about coming back to play with the Mavericks.

"He just organized this kind of unofficial minicamp that they had out here in LA with the beach yoga in Santa Monica and the runs. He's been hooping all summer long, looks like himself on Instagram and the people I know that or I've talked to that have been in the gyms with him say, 'Dude, Kyrie is Kyrie.'

"They expect him to come back and be the dude that he was a year and a half ago when he got hurt, which he was playing at at an All-NBA level."

Will the New York Knicks enter opening night without getting a deal done with Karl-Anthony Towns? How hard should Towns push in negotiations? What options would be available next summer?

Oct. 5

Clippers' Strus suffered partial tear in right foot
During Sunday's preseason game, LA Clippers guard Max Strus suffered a partial tear of the plantar fascia in his right foot, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. He will be reevaluated in four weeks.

Knicks' Karl-Anthony Towns not expecting extension soon
New York Knicks center Karl-Anthony Towns said Monday that, "It don't look good" in regards to him and the franchise agreeing to a contract extension before the start of the season.

"Simply put, I want to do something that can keep the team together and work with the Knicks and also values me," Towns said. "None of those things have come close to happening."

Towns is eligible for a four-year deal worth over $276 million.

"This is a growing cloud around the New York Knicks," ESPN's Shams Charania said on NBA Today. "So far, these sides are not close"

Oct. 2

Hawkins, Grizzlies mutually agree to part ways
The Memphis Grizzlies and guard Jordan Hawkins have agreed to part ways via waivers, allowing the 2023 lottery pick to find a new home in free agency, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

The move comes three weeks after arriving as part of a four-player trade with the New Orleans Pelicans for AJ Johnson and Taj Gibson.

Hawkins, 24, averaged 5.1 points in 51 games last season and struggled to find consistent playing time in New Orleans' crowded backcourt rotation. The former UConn star played just 13.6 minutes per game, a significant decrease from the 2024-25 season, when he played 23.6 minutes per game and averaged 10.8 points per game.

Slater on the Warriors' options this season: "I think we mentioned it last time we talked about the Warriors, but think about what the Lakers did with LeBron. I know we just questioned some of the deals they signed, but the fact that they could sign all those deals was because LeBron James took all his money and walked away. So you could let Jimmy [Butler] somewhat walk away.

"The other thing is, Jimmy and the Warriors really are fond of each other and we'll see what he looks like when he does come back. Obviously Jimmy's going to want every dollar he can get, but there's a chance Jimmy and Draymond [Green] could take pay cuts next season, right? The market might demand that they do.

"Jimmy fits really well with Steph Curry. We've seen that. Draymond is another player that you're going to hear a lot of noise about in the first week of camp from the Warriors about shifting Draymond's role and some of the numbers last year. With Draymond and Steph Curry on the floor together, it was still plus-105 last year, still a good offensive rating,117.7, but the moment Steph's been off the floor, and last year he was off the floor a lot, their offense cratered when Draymond was on the floor and was actually OK when it was no Draymond and no Steph.

"I've had these conversations with Steve [Kerr] and again I think you're going to hear it a lot publicly in their messaging, they're going to adapt the offense at times away from Draymond. They're going to try to make him more of a spot-up shooter at times instead of giving him the ball. They're trying to limit his turnovers."

Oct. 1

Duren, Pistons end standoff with long-term deal
All-NBA center Jalen Duren has agreed to a five-year, $200 million fully guaranteed contract to return to the Detroit Pistons, his agent told ESPN's Shams Charania. Duren had until 11:59 p.m. ET Thursday to decide on the Pistons' one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer.

Mitch Johnson excited about Billy Donovan's role with Spurs
San Antonio Spurs coach Mitch Johnson likes what he's seen so far at training camp from new lead assistant coach Billy Donovan.

"I don't want to be naive enough to think I'm going to tell you what a 61-year old Hall of Fame coach like Billy Donovan and his resume can bring to the table," Johnson said. "I'm excited he's here. He's a tremendous person, great personality, fits in seamlessly. He's got worlds of experience and he's an extremely hard worker. He's not kicking up his feet and telling stories. He's rolling his sleeves up and getting his hands dirty. He's going to help all of us and probably me, specifically, a ton this year."

Donovan joined the staff in July, replacing former lead assistant Sean Sweeney, who left San Antonio to take the head coaching job in Orlando. Sweeney ran the Spurs' defense last season, helping it improve from 25th to third in the NBA in defensive rating (110.4).

Donovan won't be tasked with taking on Sweeney's responsibilities, according to sources, however. San Antonio brought in Donovan to lean on his experience on both ends of the floor, as well as his vast knowledge of the NBA and college games.

A member of the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame class of 2025, Donovan joined the Spurs after 11 seasons as an NBA coach with the Chicago Bulls and Oklahoma City Thunder, after capturing two college basketball national titles in 2006 and 2007 with the Florida Gators. -- Michael C. Wright

Shead agrees to three-year extension in Toronto
Guard Jamal Shead has agreed to a three-year, $24 million extension with the Toronto Raptors, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Shead averaged 6.6 points and 5.6 assists per game last season.

Sept. 30

Nuggets add Nembhard on two-way deal

Guard Ryan Nembhard has agreed to a two-way contract with the Denver Nuggets, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Nembhard, 23, played 60 games (27 starts) for the Dallas Mavericks in 2025-26 after signing as an undrafted free agent. He was traded to the Atlanta Hawks then to the Charlotte Hornets this offseason before being waived.

Sept. 29

Charania: NBA reviewing finalists' bids for Vegas team

ESPN's Shams Charania reported that the NBA is currently reviewing finalist bids for a new expansion team in Las Vegas. The price range is currently speculated at $12-13 billion with a new arena factored into the cost.

The three final groups are Nancy Walton Laurie and Bill Laurie; Steve Apostolopoulos and Marc Lasry; Bill Foley and Jerry Colangelo, sources told ESPN.

Will KAT take a pay cut in next Knicks deal?

On "NBA Today," ESPN's Malika Andrews detailed Karl-Anthony Towns' mindset toward contract negotiations with the defending champion New York Knicks.

"Towns, from what I have been told, is willing -- similarly to what Jalen Brunson did [but the] numbers aren't the same -- to take a pay cut," Andrews said. "But the pay cut that the Knicks are asking him to take, he views as unreasonable."

Towns, 30, is eligible to sign a four-year, $276 million extension through June 30.

Embiid "full participant" in first Sixers' practice
Joel Embiid was a "full participant all the way through" for the Philadelphia 76ers first practice of training camp, Sixers coach Nick Nurse said Tuesday.

"He looked great," Nurse said of Embiid. "Very, very good news from the standpoint of where it's been the last couple years, last couple summers leading into today. ... It's great to see."

After being named the league MVP in 2023, the 32-year-old center has missed 150 games over the last three seasons because of various injuries.

He also sat out four of the Sixers' 11 playoff games in the spring because of appendicitis, right hip soreness and a right ankle sprain.

The only Sixers player who did not participate in Tuesday's practice according to a team spokesperson was backup big man Adem Bona, who is dealing with a sprained left foot.

Anfernee Simons, who signed a two-year, $12.3 million contract to join Philadelphia in July, said Embiid's presence in the gym was already notable leading up to the start of camp.

"Everybody's been impressed around here about how he's come in and worked," Simons said. "Joel is going to be Joel. He's going to be a dominant player always. We just want to continue for him to be himself, as well, and I think everybody's going to be able to work around that."

Despite the injuries, the 10-year veteran still averaged 26.9 points, 7.7 rebounds, 3.9 assists and 1.2 blocks per game last season.

Embiid's inclusion only added to what several Sixers players described as an "exciting" opening day with LeBron James and Jaylen Brown completing their first official practice with the franchise.

"With any team, we got to start somewhere, and then we got to get better and better, and just keep trying to reach our ceiling, right?" Nurse said. "That happens day-to-day. Can we get up tomorrow, like, 98% as excited as we did today? It's going to be hard to get as excited as we all were today, right?

"But we need to come back, and we need to keep climbing that mountain. That's a daily process. I just want them to reach their potential. If they do, great things are going to happen." -- Dave McMenamin

Bronny on LeBron James' Lakers exit: 'He's got his own path'

Sept. 28

Bronny on LeBron James' Lakers exit: 'He's got his own path'

When LeBron James chose to leave the Los Angeles Lakers in free agency over the summer, he consulted his family on the decision to sign with the Philadelphia 76ers. But when it came to his son/teammate Bronny, much was apparently left unsaid.

"We're men of very little words when it comes to talking about business and what we're going to do and how we feel about each other. So it wasn't really much [discussion] to be honest with you," Bronny James said Monday at Lakers media day.

"He's got his own path and I got my own. He knows that I want to make a name for myself and I want to continue my career and keep growing as a player. And he knows that I want to focus on that. So he decided to do that."

LeBron and Bronny have routinely been in unique situations in league history, whether it was opening night two years ago, when the father and son entered the game together, or last year in the playoffs, where they combined to deliver a 10-0 run during a victory over the Houston Rockets. Navigating a complex free agency in which the father leaves and the son stays is another one for the books.

Tatum 'comfortable' leading new-look Celtics post-Brown trade

Jayson Tatum's one constant during his development into a star with the Boston Celtics was having Jaylen Brown as a teammate.

That partnership ended this offseason when the Celtics' front office decided to trade Brown -- the 2024 NBA Finals MVP -- to the Philadelphia 76ers in what was largely a cost-cutting move that broke up the duo most responsible for leading Boston to the 2024 NBA championship.

"The business of the NBA comes and plays a part at some point. And I've seen it in my almost 10 years in this league," Tatum said during Celtics media day on Monday. "For me it's more so being grateful for what we accomplished and what he means for this city and to this organization. Just the ups and downs in our career that we were able to grow and learn from and made us the players that we are today. So really just being thankful for those nine years."

Suns owner Ishbia says mortgage company woes won't hurt team
It's well-known at this point that billionaire Mat Ishbia's mortgage company has had a rough financial stretch.

The owner of the Phoenix Suns said Monday that will have "zero" effect on his spending habits when it comes to basketball. In fact, the 46-year-old said he's working on purchasing 14% more of the team, bringing his total to roughly 80%.

Ishbia's company -- United Wholesale Mortgage -- suffered a reported $450 million net loss in the second quarter this year, calling into question if the sizable dip would affect his basketball business. The outspoken Ishbia was adamant that nothing would change for the NBA franchise when it comes to spending on players or the fan experience.

Williamson not where he wants to be
New Orleans Pelicans forward Zion Williamson kept his answer brief when asked how he would summarize his first seven years as an NBA player.
"I'm not where I want to be," said Williamson, whom the Pelicans drafted with the No. 1 pick out of Duke in 2019. "I'm not where I need to be."

Butler indicates he is 'ahead' in his knee rehab

Nearing the eight-month mark since his right ACL surgery, Jimmy Butler III is hesitant to put a specific target date on his eventual NBA return, but he did express optimism in advance of Golden State Warriors training camp.

"I promise you I'm coming back, and it's going to be -- I think it's going to be, like, real eye-popping for everybody how I'm still going to be nice," Butler said. "Probably nicer, honestly."

Butler has only recently advanced to running, and he will be limited to light on-court individual work when the team begins practice in Hawaii on Tuesday afternoon.

It will be several weeks before Butler is expected to advance to a more rigorous stage of his rehab, and the team's lead medical decision-maker, Rick Celebrini, is known for his cautiousness in the later stages of the rehab process.

A January or February return can be considered on the optimistic side for Butler, who turned 37 earlier this month. But Butler did say that the strengthening tests on the knee indicate he is ahead of schedule.

"My numbers are staggering," Butler said. "They're off the charts. I'm ahead, so they say. So, I just know that all the work that I've been doing, whether it be at home, in L.A., in Europe, in South America, wherever the case may be, I've been doing all the right things. So, I am confident that whenever I come back, I'll be more than ready, I'll be more than healthy and I'll be a better all-around player than I was whenever I went down." -- Anthony Slater

Pistons eye "better version" of Cunningham

Detroit Pistons coach J.B. Bickerstaff has held many offseason conversations with All-NBA guard Cade Cunningham about seizing greatness and the necessary steps toward improving after last year's playoff run that stretched to Game 7 of the Eastern Conference semifinals.

Bickerstaff has guaranteed "a better version" Cunningham this season, which could be a scary sight after he averaged 23.9 points, 9.9 assists, 5.5 rebounds and 1.4 steals in 33.9 minutes during 2025-26. But Cunningham also led the East in turnovers per game after finishing with the second most in 2024-25.

"I don't have to challenge Cade, and that's why he is who he is," Bickerstaff said. "Because he's pulling. He's not being pushed."

Cunningham showed up in a fresh pair of Nike S.T. Charge "Detroit Tough" sneakers in Pistons colors. He will also receive his own signature Nike shoe, which is expected to debut during the second half of the season.

"I'm thankful to be in these shoes. I'm thankful to have the opportunity to represent my family in this way," Cunningham said. "Represent where I come from, but then to represent the city of Detroit.

"In a city like this, it's a blessing. I'm thankful for it, I don't take it for granted and I'm trying to make the most out of it." -- Eric Woodyard

Hornets waive former No. 8 pick Dillingham

The Charlotte Hornets are waiving guard Rob Dillingham, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Dillingham was traded from the Chicago Bulls on Saturday for Buddy Hield and cash. The Hornets created a $9.6 million trade exception with the move.

Dillingham, 21, appeared in 30 games for the Bulls last season, averaging 9.6 points and 2.8 assists.

SGA on chance at historic third straight MVP

At Oklahoma City Thunder media day, guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander discussed the possibility of winning a third straight NBA MVP award and whether that's something he ponders going into this season.

"No different than any other year: Try to be the best player I can be, try to implement the things I just worked on," Gilgeous-Alexander said.

"The decision for MVP is literally 82 games away. I'm not going to win the award in the first week of the season. ... That kind of recipe for me in the past has kind of worked, and I've been fortunate to win two in a row.

"We need to be laser focused on ourselves. We need to take the lessons from that [Western Conference finals] series, for sure, and we did. But it's certainly not something that we overcorrect for, because you end up chasing your shadow, and it prevents you from being your best as you move forward."

ESPN's Summer Forecast gave Gilgeous-Alexander the fourth-best chance at the 2027 MVP, behind Victor Wembanyama, Nikola Jokic and Luka Doncic. No player has won three consecutive MVPs since Larry Bird in 1984, 1985 and 1986. -- Baxter Holmes

Doncic talks LeBron exit, Lakers "championship" ceiling
Speaking to ESPN's Brian Windhorst during Los Angeles Lakers media day, guard Luka Doncic detailed his reaction to LeBron James leaving for the Philadelphia 76ers this past summer and why he thinks a successful 2026-27 includes a Lakers run to the title:

"It was kind of sad. Playing with LeBron was amazing. There's a lot of things I learned from him. ... We all know who LeBron James is."

Shams: Duren's relationship with Pistons "has fractures"

Simmons "didn't touch a ball for a year"

During Sacramento Kings media day, guard Ben Simmons laid out the reasons he chose the Kings and why he's excited for the 2026-27 season.

"The expectations are low. I feel like that's been something on me too, so we can relate in that way," Simmons told reporters. "I think we have a chip on our shoulder."

Simmons last played in 2024-25, appearing in 51 games for the Brooklyn Nets and LA Clippers. The three-time All-Star said the time away gave him the chance to focus on "getting my body right and my mind right."

Pistons GM hasn't spoken with Duren all summer

Jalen Duren and the Detroit Pistons have a decision to make as the clock ticks closer to Oct. 1 -- the deadline to sign a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer.

For Duren, he can accept the five-year, $200 million contract that has been offered by Detroit or he can become the first player named All-NBA or All-Star to sign the qualifying offer. If he chooses the latter, Duren will hold veto power on any trade this season and be an unrestricted free agent next summer.

For the Pistons, weighing the risk of having an All-NBA player on a one-year contract and, more importantly, the likelihood he will depart next summer as a free agent is key.

There are eight projected teams that have significant cap space to sign Duren to a four-year, $189 million max contract.

"I can't control the different things that he does or his group does," Pistons president of basketball operations Trajan Langdon said at media day. "For me, it's control what we can and letting him know he is a big part of what we do."

Langdon also said he hasn't spoken with Duren all summer during Pistons media day. -- Bobby Marks

Mitchell: LeBron to Cavs made sense "for a lot of reasons"

At Cavaliers media day, Donovan Mitchell said that in his mind, he thought LeBron James would return to Cleveland because "for a lot of reasons it made sense."

"I didn't think Philly. I thought if he didn't come here, it'd be Golden State," Mitchell said.

After being swept in the Eastern Conference finals by the eventual champion New York Knicks then missing out on James in free agency, Cleveland kept its core intact. The Cavs signed Mitchell to a four-year, $273 million maximum extension and re-signed James Harden to a three-year, $97 million contract. Cleveland did make one major addition by acquiring Peyton Watson from the Denver Nuggets in a multiteam trade then signing the restricted free agent to a four-year, $88 million deal.

Speaking for the first time since their extensions, Mitchell and Harden both said their approaches to their new deals -- Mitchell signing as soon as he was eligible with Harden opting out to give Cleveland more flexibility to make moves -- reflected a team-first mindset.

"This is something that I want to do, and I want to win a championship," Harden said. "So, what does that look like? Making the team better, making the team whole to where we give ourselves a chance. By the way, you can have the best talented team, which I've been on before, and still not win.

"We waited, waited, waited until the front office called me, made sure that we got everything that we can get, and then we signed. We got a long way to go, but I love the direction and steps that we're taking here as a unit from top to bottom." -- Daniel Oyefusi

MacMahon: Thunder adjusting to roster changes
The departures of three championship-winning teammates doesn't yet feel like reality for Thunder superstar Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, who kidded that he still expected Luguentz Dort, Isaiah Joe and Aaron Wiggins to show up for Oklahoma City's team picture Monday afternoon.

"It's the business of the NBA, right?" Gilgeous-Alexander said, referring to the series of financially motivated trades. "I don't think anybody has played with all 12 guys their whole career. It sucks a little bit.

"My mind never even went to what we were going to be like on the court. It was more like the brotherhood."

As fellow OKC guard Jalen Williams added, "It's the weirdest thing ever." -- Tim MacMahon

Clippers announce Ingram has partially torn Achilles

The LA Clippers announced they found a partially torn Achilles tendon in Brandon Ingram's foot after his recent heel surgery. He will miss the start of the 2026-27 season.

Jokic: "I'm gonna sign next year"

Denver Nuggets center Nikola Jokic reiterated his commitment to the franchise at Monday's media day.

"I'm gonna sign next year," Jokic said. "If they want me."

Curry said knee is ready to go for the season

Golden State Warriors superstar guard Stephen Curry addressed the media Monday in offering positive updates on his injured knee.

"Knee's feeling great. Ready to go. No issues," Curry said. "I feel a lot stronger and understanding of what I'm dealing with."

Curry did acknowledge a "management element" but said there are currently no restrictions.

Nuggets confident in Jokic's future with franchise

Members of the Denver Nuggets' front office, general manager Jon Wallace and executive vice president of basketball Ben Tenzer addressed the media on Monday and answered questions regarding Nikola Jokic's future with the franchise. The three-time MVP didn't sign an extension this offseason.

"We feel very comfortable with the relation and trust there," Tenzer said. "We have no concerns."

LeBron: I wanted to finish my career with the Knicks
New Philadelphia 76er LeBron James said his decision came down to five teams this offseason and that he envisioned going to the New York Knicks before they won the 2026 title.

"I had visions of playing in [Madison Square] Garden and finishing my career in the Garden," James told ESPN on Monday during the 76ers' media day. "One of the best places I've ever played.

"I think it's the No. 1 arena in the world, as far as for a basketball player. But after they beat San Antonio, I was like, 'Hey, I can't.' I couldn't do it."

James and the 76ers will play the Knicks at the Garden on opening night, Oct. 20.

No update on Gary Trent Jr. investigation

Milwaukee Bucks governor Wes Edens did not provide an update on the league investigation into Gary Trent Jr.'s contract.

"I don't have any update," Edens said. "We're working with the league and fully cooperating with them. But I don't have any insight beyond that."

The NBA is looking into a potential cap-circumvention violation by the Bucks around Trent's deal this offseason.

Cronin: Blazers have "belief" in Ja Morant
Portland Trail Blazers' general manager Joe Cronin addressed why the franchise decided to trade for Ja Morant this offseason during Portland's media day on Monday.

"Just straight belief in Ja," Cronin said. "Our view of Ja as still a very high-level player.

"I'm sure there will be questions about fit, but we're very focused on talent."

Cronin also said veteran guard Jrue Holiday could play some minutes on the wing for Portland this season, while adding that Holiday and veteran guard Damian Lillard will have a positive influence on Morant.

Kerr: Rookie Lendeborg going to "play a ton"

Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr said during Monday's media day that he expects rookie Yaxel Lendeborg to "play a ton" this season.

"He's clearly going to play a ton," Kerr said. "He gives us the size and the versatility that we need.

"Whether he's a starter or coming off the bench, that will be determined the next couple of weeks."

Lendeborg was the No. 11 pick in the 2026 NBA draft and averaged 15.1 points per game at Michigan last season.

Embiid: 'Extremely excited' about this year's team
Philadelphia 76ers center Joel Embiid said Monday that he feels like the team finally has the right mix of players, after an offseason in which the franchise traded for Jaylen Brown and signed LeBron James to join the young guard tandem of VJ Edgecombe and Tyrese Maxey.

"It's hard to win when you get a group of guys together for one year, two years, maybe," he said. "I'm extremely excited about this team because we have the right mix of veteran leadership and younger guys. We might have some ups and downs, but we're gonna get there."

Wembanyama addresses last year's Finals loss
After leading by double digits in each of the five games in last season's NBA Finals, San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama said his memories of it will fuel the team this season.

"I couldn't imagine a better motivation," he said.

Harper addresses role for coming season
After offseason chatter about his role, San Antonio Spurs guard Dylan Harper said he'd follow the coaches' lead this season.

"Everyone has a competitive edge to them. But the biggest thing for me is whatever I can do, just like last year, to help the team win," he said. "Whatever position the coaches think is best for me to be in, that's the position I'll happily go in."

First look at LeBron in a 76ers uniform
New Philadelphia 76ers forward LeBron James is taking questions from reporters on Monday. Here's what he had to say when asked about his initial impressions of his team:

"Everybody is on the same page," James said. "We are all speaking the same language."

LeBron addressed his role too, saying he's open to whatever the team needs from him to win.

"Whatever they need me to do," he said. "The luxury of my game is I can do everything. ... Literally, I can do everything"

Kawhi: I was a distraction, ready to move forward
In his first public appearance with the Toronto Raptors after a controversy-filled summer, Kawhi Leonard addressed the NBA's investigation into him and his business dealings.

"I know why some of you guys came. You want to hear about the investigation. But in talking with the NBA and PA, I think the best decision is to move forward and focus on my time being a Toronto Raptor," he said. "I already was a distraction for the past 70 days and wasn't able to meet my teammates or do any of that stuff, minicamp stuff, so, moving forward, I just want to talk about the Toronto Raptors."

Haliburton: I am 100% healthy
Indiana Pacers guard Tyrese Haliburton said Monday that he is healthy and ready for the season.

"I am healthy. I am 100%," he said. "There will be no restrictions. That is not news. There is no source. I am the source. I am ready to go for the year."

Porzingis out indefinitely in blow to Warriors
Golden State Warriors big man Kristaps Porzingis is out indefinitely to open training camp with a health issue, according to the team.
In late July, Porzingis agreed to a two-year, $40 million contract with a player option on the second season to return to the Warriors.

Brown: KAT, Hart extension talks won't be a distraction
After reports surfaced last week that negotiations between the New York Knicks and center Karl-Anthony Towns had hit a stalemate, coach Mike Brown said Monday neither Towns' situation nor Hart's would linger in the locker room.

"We talk about everything [with the team]," Brown said. "We don't want to have any elephants in the room."

"I'm not involved in it. They'll figure it out. Control what you can control."

And here's what Towns said about a potential extension: "I've made it known I want to play here. Been a fan since I was a kid. I'd like to get it done."

Hornets GM: Brandon Miller to be ready for training camp
After undergoing offseason surgery on his left shoulder, Hornets wing Brandon Miller should be a full participant in training camp and "ready to roll" for opening night, Hornets general manager Jeff Peterson said Monday.

Miller, 23, is entering his fourth NBA season after being the No. 2 pick in the 2023 draft.

Duren won't be at Pistons media day, start of camp
Detroit Pistons All-Star center Jalen Duren is not attending the team's media day on Monday or the start of training camp as his contract standoff continues, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania on Monday.

Duren, a restricted free agent, is declining the team's five-year, $200 million fully guaranteed offer as both sides remain at a stalemate ahead of the Thursday deadline on a one-year, $9.6 million qualifying offer, sources said.

Bulls trade Dillingham to Hornets for Hield, cash
The Chicago Bulls and Charlotte Hornets agreed to a trade sending Rob Dillingham to Charlotte for Buddy Hield and cash, the teams announced Saturday.

What's next for Curry and the Warriors?
Stephen Curry's two-year, $116 million extension made him the first player in NBA history to amass $600 million in career on-court earnings.

The deal has also put the Golden State Warriors in position to have extra spending power next summer.

By Curry taking $10 million less than the maximum allowed, the Warriors project to have nearly $38 million in cap space in 2027. Golden State could increase its projection to $55 million if center Kristaps Porzingis is waived in the offseason. Porzingis' $20 million salary for next season is guaranteed for $3 million.

For Golden State to have ample room, forwards Draymond Green and Jimmy Butler III would need to sign elsewhere or at a significantly lesser salary. They will be free agents next summer.

Both salary projections include the $17 million free agent hold of guard Brandin Podziemski. The 2023 first-round pick is eligible until Oct. 19 to extend his contract. -- Bobby Marks

Grading the Curry deal: Why Warriors don't get an A

Hornets star Knueppel sidelined by hamstring injury
The Charlotte Hornets announced that Kon Knueppel will be out for at least the entire preseason because of a left hamstring injury.

James: Maxey, Embiid were factors in joining 76ers
LeBron James said his longstanding friendship with All-Star Tyrese Maxey and a desire to help Joel Embiid win his first NBA title played significant roles in his decision to sign a two-year, $8 million contract with the Philadelphia 76ers in July.

"[Embiid has] done everything in our league, and the only thing he has not done is win a championship. And I want to try to help him get that first one," James said. "He has a city on his back. He's been 'The Process' for 10 years, 12 years, however long he's been there. But I think it's time we even get you deeper into the process. And I hope that I can be, kind of, that final little piece that can help him get over the hump."

Grizzlies waive Russell
The Memphis Grizzlies have waived D'Angelo Russell, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Russell has made one All-Star team during his career and was selected No. 2 in the 2015 NBA draft.

stories.headline: Dream rule out top scorer Allisha Gray (finger) for Game 2
stories.summary: Dream guard Allisha Gray was ruled out of Game 2 of their semifinal series against the Liberty due to a finger injury and is considered day-to-day.
stories.body:
ATLANTA -- Atlanta Dream guard Allisha Gray was ruled out of Wednesday's Game 2 of their semifinal series against the New York Liberty due to a finger injury and is considered day-to-day, coach Karl Smesko told reporters on Tuesday.

Gray had an X-ray on her finger, though Smesko did not share any additional info on the nature or severity of her injury. Guard Rhyne Howard characterized the update as "good news."

Smesko said he anticipates Gray -- who was not present at practice on Tuesday -- to be with the team for Wednesday's game, and teammates said she was in good spirits.

"Nobody's going to try to be Lish because, I mean, there's only one Lish," Smesko said. "Lish is one of the best players in the league. She's an exceptional scorer and she's an excellent defender. So being without her for a game is tough, but we have players that are ready to step up.

"It's not who you don't have; it's how well do the players who are on the floor, how well are they able to execute the game plan, and how well are they able to play? And I expect our team to play really well."

Gray exited Sunday's 92-82 Game 1 win at the end of the first quarter with a left, shooting hand injury before returning in the second and then reinjuring it. She was ruled out for the remainder of the game shortly before halftime, scoring seven points in her 11 minutes on the floor.

The 6-foot guard and four-time All-Star out of South Carolina was the Dream's top scorer this season, averaging 19.0 points, 3.5 rebounds, 2.6 assists and 1.4 steals per game, while appearing in all 44 contests. She was also their top scorer (22.0 PPG) during a first-round sweep of the No. 5 seed Washington Mystics as Atlanta secured its first semifinals berth since 2018.

"Obviously knowing that Lish will be out, it hurts, it sucks," forward Naz Hillmon said. "I know how much she would want to be on the floor with us. We know how much we use her offensively and defensively. But that next woman up mentality is for everybody. Not just the players coming off the bench or whoever's going to fill in her role, nobody's going to be able to do what Allisha Gray does.

"We all know that, but we can all put a little bit more on our plate, and that's what our mentality is."

stories.headline: Sam McDowell, inspiration for 'Cheers' character, dies at 84
stories.summary: Sam McDowell, who led the AL in strikeouts four times before becoming a counselor for athletes suffering from addiction and depression, has died at 84.
stories.body:
CLEVELAND -- Sam McDowell, a six-time All Star who led the American League in strikeouts four times before becoming a counselor for athletes suffering from addiction issues and depression, died Monday at his home in The Villages, Florida. He was 84.

McDowell's baseball career and post-career sobriety served as the inspiration for the Sam Malone character from the iconic television sitcom "Cheers."

"Sam spent eleven of his fifteen seasons in a Cleveland uniform as one of the game's most feared hurlers. A strikeout king. He was a cherished member of our Alumni Ambassador program and loved sharing stories with our fans when he visited Progressive Field. Most importantly, Sam's life was a story of redemption," Guardians senior vice president of public affairs Bob DiBiasio said in a statement.

McDowell had a 15-year career in the major leagues from 1961-74, including 11 in Cleveland. The left-hander had a 141-134 record in 425 games, including 346 starts. He had 2,453 strikeouts, 103 complete games and 23 shutouts. McDowell also pitched for San Francisco, the New York Yankees and Pittsburgh.

In 1965, McDowell went 17-11 and led the American League in ERA (2.18) and strikeouts (325). He was 20-12 in 1970 and led the AL in both strikeouts (304) and walks (131). Cleveland traded him to San Francisco after the 1971 season.

McDowell's 9.21 strikeouts per nine innings remains a Cleveland franchise record and his 2,159 strikeouts with the club are second. He was inducted in the franchise's hall of fame in 2006.

McDowell said in his 2022 autobiography that he attempted suicide in 1963, but he survived because when he pulled the trigger, it was on the lone dead shell among live rounds in the chamber. He quit drinking in 1980 and went on to earn an associate's degree in sports psychology and addictions from the University of Pittsburgh after entering rehab.

He was certified as a counselor two years later and was a recovery consultant for the Baseball Assistance Team (B.A.T.). He was recognized with the B.A.T Lifetime Achievement Award in 2022.

stories.headline: Matchmaking, inactivity -- and, yes, fights -- shift MMA divisional rankings
stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.
stories.body:
The fighter who won a UFC championship on Saturday does not move an inch in the ESPN divisional rankings. But several other fighters who did not even compete over the weekend do rise in their divisions' top 10s. One shifts from the top of one division's rankings to the middle of the pack in another weight class.

The new champion is Natalia Silva, who cruised past unranked Wang Cong at UFC 332 to capture the vacant women's flyweight title. Silva stays put at No. 2, however, below Valentina Shevchenko, who vacated the title while recovering from injury.

Several other weight classes saw significant shifts, in some cases because of a lack of fights and in one case because of a fight booking for the future.

The most significant move is Alex Pereira shifting into the heavyweight rankings following the UFC's announcement that he will face Sergei Pavlovich on Dec. 12. It will be the second straight heavyweight fight for the former middleweight and light heavyweight champion, who has been No. 1 in the 205-pound rankings. He now moves to the heavyweight top 10, where he is ranked No. 7, two spots behind Pavlovich.

At light heavyweight, everyone previously below Pereira moves up, with ex-champion Magomed Ankalaev now No. 1. New to the top 10 are ninth-ranked Bogdan Guskov and No. 10 Robert Whittaker, as Khalil Rountree Jr. is out because he has not fought in over a year.

Also ineligible because of inactivity is middleweight Nassourdine Imavov, who is replaced in the 185-pound rankings by Christian Leroy Duncan. Perfect timing, as Duncan fights No. 5 Brendan Allen on Saturday's UFC card.

The other top-10 newcomer is men's bantamweight Payton Talbott, who knocked out Deiveson Figueiredo at UFC 332 to oust him from the rankings.

stories.headline: George Russell's F1 engine nightmare to continue with Singapore GP grid penalty - sources
stories.summary: George Russell is set to start Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix from the back of the grid as a knock-on effect of his engine failure at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, sources have told ESPN.
stories.body:
George Russell is set to start Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix from the back of the grid as a knock-on effect of his engine failure at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, sources have told ESPN.

The Mercedes driver retired from third place at Sepang due to a mechanical failure with six laps to go, delivering a critical blow to his title chances as teammate Kimi Antonelli extended his championship lead to 84 points.

The failure means Mercedes will need to introduce a new power unit to Russell's car at this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, sources have told ESPN, taking the British driver over his quota of power unit components for the season and resulting in a grid penalty.

As a cost-saving measure in F1's regulations, each car is only allowed a set number of power unit components for the season, with additional usage resulting in grid drops at the next grand prix.

After reliability issues earlier this year, Mercedes had already planned for Russell to take an additional power unit before the end of the season but was not planning for him to do so in Singapore where overtaking is notoriously difficult.

However, the failure in Malaysia has forced the team's hand as Russell does not have enough sufficiently low-mileage parts in his pool of power unit components to avoid taking a fresh engine this weekend.

- Singapore Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch

- Bahrain GP was the worst indictment of F1's new engine regs yet

- Could Malaysia return to F1 calendar? The state of play

Mercedes is set to bring a performance upgrade to its power unit before the end of the year, which it had originally hoped to coincide with the introduction of Russell's final power unit of the year.

The team has not yet confirmed whether the upgrade -- granted under the FIA's Additional Development Upgrade Opportunity (ADUO) catch-up mechanism -- can be fast-tracked for introduction in Singapore.

If it is not possible to use the ADUO upgrade in Singapore, Mercedes will then face the decision of whether to take a further grid penalty with Russell later in the year to put the upgraded power unit in his car.

Antonelli has already used one additional power unit beyond his season-long quota, which resulted in a grid penalty at the Italian Grand Prix. Despite starting 19th at Monza, the championship leader went on to win the race.

North Melbourne has named Jaymie Graham as its next head coach, tasking the Fremantle assistant with lifting the Kangaroos off the bottom of the AFL ladder.

The highly-rated Dockers assistant is understood to have addressed the Kangaroos board on Monday following an impressive presentation during the selection process.

stories.headline: State of each position in 2026: What are the biggest tactical trends?
stories.summary: Elite soccer has changed dramatically in recent years, and the most valued player skill sets have evolved as a result.
stories.body:
Elite European soccer in 2026 feels decidedly different from what we've become used to. Over the past couple of seasons, the Premier League has been increasingly characterized by direct attacking, set pieces and long throw-ins. Many encounters between big clubs across Europe have become frenetic, end-to-end affairs, such as the Bayern Munich-Paris Saint-Germain semifinals in last season's UEFA Champions League.

A lot of the changes seem related to how teams play without the ball. The soccer we became accustomed to throughout the 2010s involved top sides trying to push their opponents back while keeping the ball. Once the ball reached the attacking third, they tried to outnumber defenders in key spaces and make use of their attacking talent.

One way for defensive sides to counter this approach is to use zonal marking, which involves defending space rather than individual players. They would set up in compact blocks and deny space in critical areas, whether they defended deep like Max Allegri's Juventus in the 2010s or pressed high like teams coached by Ralf Rangnick's disciples. While this tactic helps protect the areas closer to goal and prevent mismatches, it sometimes plays into the hands of those high-possession sides.

As a result, player marking (or man-to-man marking), in which defenders are assigned to follow attackers around up and down the pitch, started to make a comeback at the turn of the 2020s. Teams like Mikel Arteta's Arsenal and Andoni Iraola's Bournemouth combined this concept with their zonal marking, switching out of a zonal structure in certain situations to swarm teams attempting to move the ball forward (hybrid pressing). This makes moving the ball slowly up the pitch harder, causing teams to embrace more direct approaches with the ball.

Meanwhile, the game appears to be becoming more physical and more intense. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, every passing season of the Premier League has seen faster sprinting and more "high-intensity actions." And with off-ball physical data like running distance or top speed becoming more accessible, scouting departments now possess more transparent measures of athleticism, leading to players' athletic qualities being valued more.

Rather than just affecting the head coach's team talk, these big-picture changes have a major effect on the skill sets that clubs look for when assembling their starting XIs. Let's take a look at five positions -- goalkeepers, center backs, fullbacks, central midfielders, and strikers -- to see what has changed and why.

Goalkeepers: Distribution and cross-claiming

New Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki has generated much buzz this season. One of his standout features has been his passing ability, playing quick passes to his center backs during the early buildup and exquisite floated long passes to Villa's forwards to escape pressure.

As impressive as his reflex saves are, Suzuki doesn't appear to be a great shot stopper. His "goals prevented" stats, based on post-shot expected goals, reveal that his shot-stopping numbers have hovered around that of the average major league goalkeeper over the past couple of seasons. In fact, in 2025-26, he prevented minus-0.4 goals per 90 minutes, implying that he did slightly worse than the average keeper last season.

However, his passing displays and his excellent cross-claiming make him a highly prized player, and his skill set epitomizes the state of today's goalkeeping.

When Pep Guardiola's Manchester City signed Gianluigi Donnarumma -- known for his shot-stopping abilities, but arguably an average distributor -- as their first-choice goalkeeper in summer 2025, it looked like elite soccer was once again prioritizing shot-stopping between the sticks. But the tactical conditions of soccer in the 2020s make ball-playing goalkeepers even more crucial than before; when teams are tasked with playing the ball past intense man-to-man presses, goalkeepers have more to do in the buildup phase.

Even the most aggressive man-to-man presses don't generally mark the goalkeeper, making keepers free options in the buildup. From this point, keepers are instrumental to playing quick passes around the box to try to bait the press for "artificial transitions" as well as with playing longer passes into space to relieve pressure and kick-start a direct attack.

As a result, the heyday of keepers primarily known for what they can do with their feet looks unlikely to recede anytime soon, with more intense pressing and more direct attacking arguably magnifying their value.

Meanwhile, although the number of open-play crosses that teams in the Big Five leagues play has decreased slightly since 2018, the ever-rising threat of set-play goals makes cross-claiming an especially valuable skill. The first-choice keepers at big clubs dominate the top of the leaderboard for cross-claiming statistics; Donnarumma ranked No. 1 for the highest percentage of crosses claimed in the Premier League last season, Barcelona's Joan García and Real Madrid's Thibaut Courtois ranked second and third, respectively, in last season's LaLiga campaign, and PSG's Lucas Chevalier ranked third in Ligue 1.

On the other hand, the keepers who populated the bottom of cross-claiming tables belong to either lower-table clubs or underperforming established sides like Tottenham Hotspur and Newcastle United. As valuable as goalkeepers' distribution is in 2026, it appears that the ability to claim crosses has become crucial to success between the sticks.

Center backs: Playmaking and pushing forward

In the 2015-16 Premier League season, the top five players who completed the most passes per 90 were Santi Cazorla, Cesc Fabregas, Bastian Schweinsteiger, Aaron Ramsey and Michael Carrick, with more central and attacking midfielders completing the top 10. In 2025-26, the top five were Rodri, Lewis Dunk, Curtis Jones, Trevoh Chalobah and William Saliba, with seven center backs making up the top 10.

A decade ago, central midfielders were at the heart of elite sides' passing moves, but today, especially in the Premier League, center backs are the primary passers in most sides.

In the Big Five leagues, center backs completed 19% more passes in the 2025-26 season than in 2018-19. Much of this has to do with intense man-to-man pressing systems, meaning that players positioned deeper have more prominent buildup duties. The 2020s have also seen nominal center backs become more involved in attacking play, taking up higher and wider positions. Attacking center backs are effective tools to dismantle mid-blocks, helping complicate marking duties with their movement.

This is easiest to do with wide center backs in a back three. Gian Piero Gasperini's Atalanta and Simone Inzaghi's Internazionale did this especially often. This season, Xabi Alonso's Chelsea and Gasperini's AS Roma are key examples, with the latter probably representing the most adventurous iteration of attacking center backs we've seen this century.

We can see some of this in back-four systems, too. Guardiola used John Stones as a center back who roved forward in possession at City, while Thiago Motta used Riccardo Calafiori and Jhon Lucumí as center backs with free roles.

As this decade progresses, the phrase "center back" might be encased in quotation marks more often.

Fullbacks: Rise of the underlap

Fullbacks often epitomize the tactical eras they find themselves in. The turn of the 2010s saw the rise of overlapping attacking fullbacks who move high up the pitch and outside wingers who cut inside with the ball. The mid-to-late 2010s saw the rise of high-intensity pressing, with high-possession sides using inverted fullbacks to provide security against counterattacks resulting from losing the ball. Meanwhile, the relative conservatism that followed the COVID-19 pandemic meant that nominal center backs were often deployed at fullback.

Today, we're seeing the rise of attacking fullbacks who underlap, making runs into the channels between opposition fullbacks and center backs, much like inverted wingers. As Caleb Gearty notes for SCOUTED, "the ability to receive the ball" is progressively becoming more highly valued for fullbacks. After getting in behind back lines, underlapping fullbacks can put in dangerous cutbacks and crosses from closer to goal, or take shots themselves.

In the case of back-three formations, this isn't a new phenomenon. For instance, Thomas Tuchel's Chelsea saw wingbacks Reece James and Ben Chilwell move inside and score goals, while Inzaghi used Federico Dimarco and Denzel Dumfries as goal-scoring threats at Inter.

But now, fullbacks in back-four systems are increasingly venturing forward and inside -- not just putting crosses in, but getting on the end of goal-scoring opportunities, too. Arsenal's Calafiori and Manchester City's Nico O'Reilly often make darting runs into the box and offer secondary goal threats. Spain's World Cup win saw Marc Cucurella and Pedro Porro underlap, pulling defenses apart.

Meanwhile, back-three systems feature wingbacks who pose greater goal-scoring threats than ever. Alonso's Chelsea are an instructive example -- they signed Pep Chavarría and Marco Palestra, but Alonso currently appears to favor the left-footed winger Pedro Neto at right wingback, who makes sharp runs into the box.

Why is this the case? In an age when defensive tactics are dominated by player-marking, the positional interchanges around the flanks (or "wide rotations") and unexpected diagonal darts forward from fullbacks can scramble player-marking duties and open up space -- especially when wingers find themselves closer to the sideline. As Billy Carpenter writes, sudden moves into the spaces in behind defenses can expose structural vulnerabilities in even the best mid-blocks.

Calafiori so far this season represents a great example, making well-timed runs in behind and receiving incisive through balls ...

... and creating goals like these.

Jamie Carragher once remarked that fullbacks are either failed wingers or failed center backs. The rise of inverted fullbacks would've allowed Carragher to add "failed midfielder" to his jibe, while today, a middling inside forward can consider a successful career as an underlapping attacking fullback.

Central midfielders: Large spaces and generalists

In 2026, the most expensive player archetype to sign in soccer appears to be the generalist midfielder. Of the 10 most expensive transfers this summer per Transfermarkt, six were central midfielders. And among the major moves in midfield that big clubs made this summer, most midfielders are do-it-all generalists who, at least in theory, contribute to passing, carrying, winning the ball back and sometimes crashing the box. These include Elliot Anderson, Sandro Tonali, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Bruno Guimarães, Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos.

This hasn't always been the case. By 2009, the box-to-box midfielder had become a dying breed, superseded by specialists in midfield. In the late 2010s, the rise of pressing meant that press-resistant ball carriers in midfield became increasingly valued, epitomized by the summer 2019 transfer window, which saw Frenkie de Jong, Tanguy Ndombele and Mateo Kovacic move for sums exceeding €40 million. But now, every big club is willing to spend astronomic sums on their own equivalent of Declan Rice or Moisés Caicedo; athletic midfielders who can cover lots of ground and do a bit of everything.

Counterintuitively, this might be happening because less of the game is happening in midfield. With the rise of situational player-marking, the middle third sees larger spaces opened up between lines of pressure, while space becomes more constricted in teams' own thirds. As a result, moving the ball from defense to midfield becomes a harder task, while the spaces opened up in the middle third mean teams don't pass the ball around as much there, instead moving the ball through it more quickly.

Jon Mackenzie and Jake Entwistle have discussed the relevance of "small spaces" -- where the player on the ball has little room to work with in the face of pressure -- and "large spaces" -- where players need to cover ground quickly, especially during transitions or when a line of pressure is broken -- in midfield, which influences how midfielder profiles are valued today. A player like Anderson, who combines small-space and large-space skills, becomes priceless, but the broader emphasis shifts from small-space specialists to large-space generalists who can cover ground and offer control in the center of the park.

As a result, affecting the pace of the attack, rather than just exerting control over space, becomes a key consideration in midfield. The rise of artificial transitions in response to pressing also means central midfielders are key to moving the ball from small spaces to large spaces, as Carlos Baleba did adeptly while at Brighton.

The middle of the park is integral to controlling a game of soccer, and as we're seeing the very notion of "control" change in the middle of the 2020s, the traits associated with the most highly valued midfielders are transformed, too.

Strikers: Physicality and pinning

While the first two decades of top-level soccer in the 21st century saw increasing versatility at the center forward position, the opposite is happening in the third decade. So far, the 2020s have seen taller, faster and stronger strikers being valued more than their smaller, more technical counterparts. Of course, Erling Haaland represents the platonic ideal of a striker -- in this era and in any other -- but the players who spearhead attacks in the middle of the 2020s tend to be 6-foot-2 or taller, and combine their size with pace.

Today's strikers are also less involved in link-up play than their equivalents at the turn of the 2020s, with the average striker in the Big Five leagues completing 16% fewer passes in 2025-26 than in 2018-19.

As discussed earlier, with attacks becoming more direct, the established strategy of pushing teams back and overwhelming defenses with patient play in the attacking third is falling out of fashion, which means strikers don't need to be as involved outside the penalty area. Instead, strikers increasingly spend most of the game pinning back defenders and stretching back lines, attempting to find space within settled defensive blocks. Plus, an increased emphasis on transitions correspondingly makes outlets to hit on the break becoming more valuable, and some extra size certainly comes in handy while trying to score goals from set pieces.

However, the players who currently lead most big clubs' front lines indicate the trend might be reversing at the upper echelons of the game. Harry Kane drops deeper than ever and conducts passing moves from midfield at Bayern, PSG won the Champions League with Ousmane Dembélé as a false 9 last season, Mikel Arteta appears to favor Kai Havertz up front over Viktor Gyokeres at Arsenal, and Barcelona currently deploy Raphinha at the No. 9 spot.

This might be because teams are finding alternate ways of manipulating player-marking strategies, picking holes in defenses with positional interchanges. By dropping deeper, a striker can bring the defender assigned to marking him along and create space for teammates. For example, in this case, João Pedro dropping deep to receive a throw-in pokes a hole for Morgan Rogers to run into, who in turn creates space for Cole Palmer's carry and goal.

For now, specialized, physically gifted strikers may have their time in the sun, but we're likely to see many approaches at the center forward position as the decade progresses.

What to make of 2026 trends

Many soccer fans view today's tactical landscape as being one of stasis or even regression. It's tempting to view the rise of directness and set pieces, as well as do-it-all midfielders and big strikers, as the return of older approaches. But this might be a reductive view; as Mackenzie notes in his book "The Spectre of Pep," presenting changes in the tactical landscape as purely being "cyclical" makes it "very difficult to speak of the 'new' in any meaningful way at all."

All the smaller tactical shifts we're seeing across the pitch are happening in relation to broader changes in the tactical environment of the 2020s. With the rise of man-to-man pressing approaches and the resulting revival of direct attacking, accompanied with the resurgence of ground-eating midfielders and big, physical strikers, these very same trends have brought about the rise of playmaking goalkeepers, attacking center backs, and underlapping fullbacks.

If a Premier League manager from 2006 drove a plutonium-powered DeLorean to 2026, he might find the first five minutes of play recognizable, but would be scandalized by the time he reaches the 10-minute mark. Welcome to elite soccer in the 2020s.

stories.headline: Five grand finalists named in Samoa's RLWC squad
stories.summary: Ben Gardiner has been denied the chance to call up Payne Haas, but Samoa's Rugby League World Cup squad remains filled with NRL talent.
stories.body:
Francis Manuleleua and Jermaine McEwen have been rewarded for their starring roles in Newcastle's run to the NRL Grand Final with the back-row duo named in Samoa's Rugby League World Cup squad.

Even without Payne Haas, as the South Sydney-bound prop undergoes hand surgery, the Samoan squad is still packed with talent.

Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Brian To'o and Stephen Crichton are all included, along with Sydney Roosters front-rower Spencer Leniu following his exploits in the NRL Grand Final.

Jarome Luai will co-captain the side with Parramatta prop Junior Paulo.

"One of the great things rugby league does is bring people together," Toa Samoa coach Ben Gardiner said.

"As we build towards our first World Cup game, we want to thank all Samoans around the world for their ongoing support.

"Your blessings and prayers are welcomed.

"Whether you are in Samoa, elsewhere around the world, taking part in a parade or marching into the ground, we see you and thank you for your love and support."

Roosters hooker Benaiah Ioelu is likely to share hooking duties with Jazz Tevaga, who won the Super League Grand Final with Wakefield last week.

Gardiner's side will open their campaign against France in Parramatta before facing Papua New Guinea in Port Moresby and rounding out their pool stage fixtures against Tonga.

Samoa squad: Shawn Blore, Stephen Crichton, Sua Fa'alogo, Clayton Faulalo, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Benaiah Ioelu, Connelly Lemuelu, Spencer Leniu, Jarome Luai, Francis Manuleleua, Deine Mariner, Ata Mariota, Greg Marzhew, Jermaine McEwen, Francis Molo, Junior Paulo, Pasami Saulo, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Izack Tago, Jazz Tevaga, Brian To'o, Enari Tuala, Ronald Volkman.

stories.headline: Fantasy football consistency ratings: 2024 to 2026
stories.summary: The consistency ratings weigh both how consistent and how start-worthy players have been from 2024 to 2026.
stories.body:
Updated Oct. 6, 2026 (through Week 4 of 2026)

How consistency ratings work
Using fantasy points determined by ESPN's standard scoring, the charts contained in this column rate players based upon how consistently reliable they have been during the 2024 through 2026 seasons, a span of 40 weeks' worth of games (18 weeks apiece in 2024 and 2025, four so far in 2026). For IDPs (individual defensive players), the scoring from our weekly rankings is used: solo tackle (1.5), assisted tackle (0.75), tackle for loss (2), sack (4), interception (5), forced fumble (4), fumble recovery (4), touchdown (6), safety (2), pass defended (1.5). To familiarize you with the terminology and column headers listed in the charts below:

Start%: The player's "start percentage," which shows how often he earned a start in an ESPN standard PPR (points per reception) league. This is his number of "starts" -- those defined below -- divided by his number of scheduled team games.

CR: The player's "consistency rating," which is calculated as his weekly standard deviation divided by his PPR fantasy points per game average. This is meant to identify the players who were most consistently close to their weekly averages. The lower the number, the more consistent the player. Again, lower numbers are better.

nPPR%: The player's start percentage using non-PPR scoring, using ESPN's standard scoring settings without any points per reception.

FPTS/G: The player's average PPR fantasy points scored per game.

Start: The number of times that the player's point total in a given week was worthy of having had him active in an ESPN standard PPR league.

Star: The number of times the player's point total ranked among the best at his position.

Stiff: The number of times the player's point total ranked among the worst at his position, making almost any waiver-wire option a smarter choice.

These are the benchmarks for what constitutes a "start," "star" or "stiff" performance:

Sat: The number of times the player sat out a game. Players are not charged "stiff" points for sitting out, nor does it impact their overall consistency rating (CR), but it hurts their overall start percentage.

Players must have a start rate of at least 20% in either standard PPR or non-PPR scoring, rank among the top 20 quarterbacks, tight ends or kickers, top 50 running backs or wide receivers, or top 40 defensive linemen, linebackers or defensive backs, in terms of total fantasy points at their position from 2024 to 2026, or are averaging at least 50 snaps per game, for inclusion in the chart.
